report.tagline: Alphabet's driverless taxi service: you hail a car in an app and it drives you with nobody in the driver's seat.
report.simpleSummary: Waymo is a robotaxi. You open the Waymo app (or Uber in some cities), request a ride, and a white Jaguar with spinning sensors on the roof arrives with no driver. It drives itself to your destination using cameras, radar, lidar and AI trained over more than 15 years. It started as Google's self-driving car project in 2009, runs paid rides in several US cities, and is expanding to 20+ cities in 2026, including London.

overview.whatItDoes: Waymo builds the self-driving software and hardware (the 'Waymo Driver') and runs its own robotaxi service, Waymo One. It operates in cities like Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin and Atlanta, partly through Uber in Austin and Atlanta. It is owned by Alphabet, Google's parent, and led by co-CEOs Tekedra Mawakana and Dmitri Dolgov.
howItWorks: Each car carries lidar (laser sensors that build a 3D map), radar and cameras that see 360 degrees.
AI software predicts what every car, cyclist and pedestrian will do and plans a safe path.
Waymo first maps a city in detail and tests for months with safety drivers before going fully driverless.
Riders book in the Waymo app or Uber app; the car arrives, unlocks for them, and they ride alone.
Remote support staff can give the car advice in odd situations, but do not drive it with a joystick.
Fleet partners like Avis and Uber-backed operators handle cleaning, charging and maintenance in some cities.
overview.valueProposition: A safe, calm, private ride with no driver to talk to or tip, at a price close to Uber, available day and night.

businessModel.summary: Waymo earns from robotaxi fares, directly in its app or shared with Uber and other partners. Later it may license its driver technology to carmakers and delivery firms. Today it spends far more than it earns, funded by Alphabet and outside investors.

revenueStreams.detail: Riders pay per trip, priced near or above Uber.
Shared fares when rides come through Uber or Lyft.
Possible licensing to carmakers like Toyota and Hyundai.

businessModel.pricing: Per-ride pricing in the app, based on distance and time. Fares are usually similar to or a bit higher than Uber for the same trip; no tipping.
costDrivers: Vehicles with expensive sensors (much more than a normal car)
Fleet operations: cleaning, charging, depots, maintenance
businessModel.unitEconomics: Rough estimate: a $20 Waymo ride has no driver cost, which is about 70% of an Uber fare. But each car may cost well over $100,000, plus depots, charging, insurance and support. With around 25 rides a day per car, it may earn $400 to $500 a day per car before covering these costs, so profit depends on lower vehicle costs and more rides per car. Alphabet has said Waymo is not expected to be financially meaningful until 2027 to 2028.

howTheyGetUsers: Word of mouth and viral social media videos
Partnership with Uber to reach riders
growth.moat: Waymo has more than 15 years of driving data and hundreds of millions of driverless miles, plus permits and a safety record regulators trust. Replicating that experience takes years. Alphabet's money lets it fund losses longer than rivals.

competitors.name: Tesla Robotaxi
competitors.positioning: Camera-only self-driving with cheaper cars, launched in Austin.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Waymo uses lidar and has years more driverless operation; Tesla may scale cheaper.

competitors.name: Zoox (Amazon)
competitors.positioning: Purpose-built robotaxi pods with no steering wheel.

competitors.name: Uber and Lyft with human drivers
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Waymo has no driver costs and a different experience but much smaller coverage.

competitors.name: Baidu Apollo Go and WeRide
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Waymo leads in the US; Chinese firms lead in China and the Middle East.

competitors.name: Wayve
competitors.positioning: UK AI driving software for carmakers, partnered with Uber in London.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Waymo runs its own fleet with lidar; Wayve licenses software that learns end to end.

pmLessons: Trust is the main product. Waymo launches slowly, city by city, because one bad crash could set it back years.
A long head start creates a moat. 15+ years of data is hard to copy.
Partnering for demand (Uber) and operations (Avis) lets you focus on your core technology.
Unit economics come later. Waymo proved the product first, and now must cut cost per car.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you choose the next city for Waymo?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weather, rules, demand, road complexity, partners. Score cities and pick one with reasons.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you get a nervous first-time rider to try Waymo?
interviewQuestions.hint: Find fears, offer free first ride, show safety data and live screen explanations. Measure first ride conversion.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Waymo run its own app or partner with Uber everywhere?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare control, data, brand vs reach and speed. Suggest a mix by city.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Waymo's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Paid driverless rides per week. Break into fleet, utilisation, demand and safety.

interviewQuestions.question: A Waymo car blocked an ambulance. As PM, what do you do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Respond fast, find root cause, fix software, share with regulators, track incidents.
